question_text: A 70-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of worsening nocturia, fatigue, and shortness of breath on exertion. While he used to be able to walk for 15 minutes at a time, he now has to pause every 5 minutes. Recently, he has started using two pillows to avoid waking up short of breath at night. He has a history of hypertension treated with daily amlodipine and prazosin; he has difficulty adhering to his medication regimen. His pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a laterally displaced apical heartbeat and 2+ bilateral pitting edema of the lower legs. Auscultation shows an S4 gallop and fine bibasilar rales. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following pathophysiologic changes in this patient?

                    ### Question
                    A 70-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of worsening nocturia, fatigue, and shortness of breath on exertion. While he used to be able to walk for 15 minutes at a time, he now has to pause every 5 minutes. Recently, he has started using two pillows to avoid waking up short of breath at night. He has a history of hypertension treated with daily amlodipine and prazosin; he has difficulty adhering to his medication regimen. His pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a laterally displaced apical heartbeat and 2+ bilateral pitting edema of the lower legs. Auscultation shows an S4 gallop and fine bibasilar rales. Further evaluation is most likely to show which of the following pathophysiologic changes in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Constriction of efferent renal arterioles
opb. Increase in urinary bicarbonate excretion
opc. Decrease in total peripheral vascular resistance
opd. Reduction of alveolar surface tension
ope. Retention of potassium

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms and examination findings are consistent with heart failure, likely heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) due to hypertension-induced left ventricular hypertrophy. In heart failure, decreased cardiac output leads to activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), which causes constriction of efferent renal arterioles to maintain glomerular filtration rate. This aligns with option 'opa' and is supported by the evidence path showing the role of RAAS in heart failure. The chain suggesting retention of potassium is incorrect; heart failure typically leads to sodium and water retention, not potassium. The evidence paths associating water with potassium uptake are misleading in this context. Increased sympathetic activity in heart failure usually results in increased peripheral vascular resistance, contradicting option 'opc'. Pulmonary congestion in heart failure causes bibasilar rales and orthopnea, but does not reduce alveolar surface tension, contradicting option 'opd'. Therefore, the most likely pathophysiologic change in this patient is 'opa': constriction of efferent renal arterioles.
